body.text: Kerala-born Nithya Raman has won the Los Angeles mayoral race, becoming the first Indian-American elected to lead the city, as incumbent Karen Bass conceded defeat and pledged a smooth transition. Raman’s victory propels the urban planner and city council member to the leadership of America’s second-largest metropolis, establishing her simultaneously as its first South Asian mayor and marking a historic milestone in a political journey that began with her election to the municipal council in 2020.

“Los Angeles, I am deeply honoured to be your next mayor,” Raman wrote on X on November 5. The outgoing municipal leader expressed her appreciation to supporters while vowing continued dedication to the city, whereas Raman noted that she had spoken with Bass to convey her appreciation for her leadership and long-standing public service.

Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory. “While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said. “I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”

Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for reelection. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades Fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.

Raman’s electoral campaign focussed intensely on housing accessibility, homelessness management and upgrading municipal services, with LAist noting that her pledges encompassed enhanced street light and pothole maintenance, alongside structural policing reforms.

With her victory, the two largest US cities, New York and Los Angeles, will have mayors of South Asian descent. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took office in January 2026, is also a Democratic Socialist.
Late entry

Raman was an 11th-hour entrant into the race and had even initially backed Bass’ re-election bid. But she made a shock decision to throw her hat in, filing in the final hours before the deadline, a decision that infuriated the city’s Democratic establishment, who had coalesced around Bass despite her shortcomings.

People are “dissatisfied” with the “broken status quo” of Los Angeles, Raman told AFP in the days before the November 3 midterm vote, which proved a night of dramatic gains for Democrats. Raman didn’t declare victory on Tuesday, as California’s notoriously slow ballot counting hadn’t yet provided a clear result.

But she did speak to thousands of supporters and appeared to believe her victory was inevitable. “This city’s government has made solving problems look impossible for so long,” said the Ivy League-educated urban planner. "Hopelessness can be fatal for a city, but this campaign refused to accept that.”
Early years

The blueprint for Raman’s political philosophy was drawn not in Los Angeles but on the streets of Chennai, along the banks of the Cooum River, and in the suburb of Nanganallur, long before headlines began celebrating her historic victory as a Democratic Socialist set to lead America’s second-largest city.

Though born in Thrissur, Keralam, to a Tamil Brahmin family that emigrated to the United States when she was about six, Raman’s political awakening appears to belong to Chennai. In 2010, with a degree from Harvard and a master’s in city planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, she did what few Ivy League graduates do: she moved back. Between 2010 and 2013, Chennai became her living laboratory.

She headed Transparent Chennai, a project under the Centre for Development Finance. It was no sterile think tank. Raman and her team walked the city’s streets with GPS devices and notebooks, doing the unglamorous groundwork of grassroots governance. Under her leadership, Transparent Chennai launched the Public Sanitation and Toilet Mapping Project.

Raman went into slum resettlement colonies and mapped public toilets by hand, exposing the gap between government claims and reality. She also built data registries of Chennai’s informal waste pickers and recyclers, and lobbied the State government to recognise their trade and include them in municipal planning.

When the state began aggressive slum evictions along Chennai’s waterways, including the Cooum, Raman stood with the urban poor. She co-authored research opposing the forced displacement of families to far-flung resettlement colonies, showing how the clearances stripped families of their livelihoods without providing basic amenities. Her work was deeply collaborative. In the southern suburb of Nanganallur, she partnered with citizen groups such as Exnora and the Thillai Ganga Nagar Residents’ Welfare Association, among them civic activists like V. Rama Rao of Lakshmi Nagar.

“The collaboration involved organising community forums, mapping local traffic issues, and collecting data on public transport, pedestrian safety, and civic infrastructure gaps to present actionable data to the Chennai Traffic Police and municipal corporations,” Rama Rao said.

A resident of Thillai Ganga Nagar recalled that she was then an urban planner and activist keen to understand traffic problems and talk to locals. “We didn’t know then that she would become a politician and mayor one day,” he said. “She taught us that data could be weaponised,” recalled a former civic volunteer from those early days, adding, “She showed us that when ordinary citizens have empirical evidence, local governments can no longer ignore them.”

Raman openly credits this framework with shaping her approach to community activism and, eventually, her mayoral campaign, which rested on the same premise: using data-driven, compassionate urban planning to tackle housing affordability and homelessness.

Having previously broken barriers as the first Asian-American woman and the first South Asian elected to the Los Angeles City Council in 2020, Raman subsequently secured a renewed mandate during the 2024 electoral cycle.
Growing political power

Indian American Impact, an organisation that empowers South Asian and Indian-American communities through community engagement, civic partnerships, and candidate support, congratulated Raman on her victory in the general election for Mayor of Los Angeles.

Noting that Raman will become the first South Asian American mayor of the nation’s second-largest city, the Indian American Impact said her victory reflects the growing political power of South Asian Americans in California, a state with more than one million South Asian residents, the largest such population in the country.
The Indian-American community’s gains

The 5.5 million-strong Indian-American community registered significant political gains in the midterms, with several candidates from the community winning historic elections to various positions across the country. Pia Dandiya of Florida and Dr Amish Shah of Arizona will be the newest Indian-American members of the US Congress, with their victories speaking to the “growing political power of our communities.” They will join Representative Ami Bera, Representative Pramila Jayapal, Representative Ro Khanna and Representative Suhas Subramanyam at Capitol Hill.

“At a time of rising hate against our communities, representation matters, and they will fight to keep our communities safe,” Indian American Impact said. “All six are committed to lowering costs for working families, expanding access to health care, and protecting immigrants, and they will serve as a powerful check on the Trump administration in the next Congress,” the organisation said.

Among the other notable election victories are those of Manoj Chourasia, who has been reelected to the New Hampshire State House; Darshana Patel, who won her reelection to the California State Assembly; and Ranjeev Puri, who won reelection to the Michigan House of Representatives.

With Democrats retaking the chamber, Puri is expected to become Michigan’s next Speaker of the House, which would make him the first Indian American Speaker of a state House in the country. Dr Krish Subrahmanian won his election for the Minnesota State Senate; Aruna Miller has been reelected as Lieutenant Governor of Maryland; Lisa Kaul won her election for the New York State Senate, defeating a Republican incumbent and flipping a seat in New York; and Nabeela Syed won her election for Illinois State Senate District 26.

Amar Mukunda won his election to the Maryland State Senate; Saba Haider has been elected to the Illinois State House; Josh Kaul has been re-elected as Wisconsin’s Attorney General; Pooja Sethi won her election to the Texas House, District 47, becoming the first Indian American to serve in the Texas legislature; and Jyot Singh has been elected to the Georgia State House, District 97, the first Indian American and first Sikh American elected to the Georgia State Legislature.
(With inputs from agencies)
